name: PT Bukit Asam (Persero) Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bukit Asam: the bridge corrected, the permit the value rests on
frontmatter.summary: We keep BUY and raise the target after the QC revision: the dividend payable that had been double-deducted against the September base is removed, the bridge now matches the balance sheet the engine reads, and the method-card outputs — cost-curve position, through-cycle price, reserve life and NAV at spot — are added. The Q4 profit step-up, permit renewal and the PLN receivable remain the cautions.
thesis: The nine-month surge is a price-and-cost story, not a volume recovery: profit more than trebled on a higher average selling price and almost flat cost of revenue while sales and production both fell.

This year's volume reconciles the nine-month sales with the production build and the third-quarter run-rate; from next year we hold the company's 49.50 Mt 2026 target as a target, not as an approved 2027 plan, and the approval risk is quantified.

The realised ratio is the coal-only ratio the nine-month print measures, not a haircut; it applies to a benchmark above the level it was measured on, and the compression unwinds to the last-actual calibration from the third forecast year.

The new export-channel rule is an administrative change to nearly half the book, not a modelled price or volume cut: DSI states it takes no margin, PTBA is aligning its systems and existing contracts continue; the unquantified service fee and a possible go-live slip are what we monitor.

The life-of-asset DCF at the coal deck's through-cycle path still values the equity well above the price, while the dividend-capacity anchor sits below it; that gap is our honest caution, not a reason to cut the rating, and renewal of the Banko Barat permit carries most of the value.

Cash conversion still has to be watched: receivables rose far faster than revenue in the nine months, led by the state power counterparty, but the ageing is disclosed only in aggregate rather than by customer, so the full-year accounts remain the test.

catalysts.event: Fourth-quarter delivery against the full-year sales target after a weak nine months
Decision on the share buyback under review since October 2026
Go-live of the single export channel through state exporter PT DSI
2027 production plan and RKAB approval after the domestic-first submission filed in October
Expiry of the Banko Barat IUP term, the permit whose renewal carries most of the DCF value
Annual GMS and FY2026 dividend determination

blocks.text: We keep our **BUY** rating with a twelve-month target of **Rp4,894**, an expected total return of **74.5%** from the 4 November close of Rp3,030 [S0]. This revision answers the QC audit, not a new event. The QC block was a double deduction: the FY2025 dividend was declared on 11 June and paid on 10 July 2026, so the 30 September balance sheet the engine reads already reflects it, and the separate dividend-payable bridge item deducted it a second time [S6]. Removing that item raises the life-of-reserve DCF by the dividend-payable amount, IDR1,304.8bn, and matches the model to the balance sheet it actually uses; the target rises with it. The method-card outputs on cost position, the through-cycle price, reserve life and NAV at spot are now stated in the industry and valuation sections [S0, S5, S7].

**What changed in the model, and what did not.** The nine-month print is unchanged — net profit IDR4,410.0bn, revenue IDR35,200.0bn and EBITDA IDR7,190.0bn [S11, S17] — and the coal deck's forward path is unchanged [S0]. What changed is how the annual build uses them. First, FY2026E volume is 47.00 Mt, because nine-month sales of 32.23 Mt sat below nine-month production of 34.41 Mt and the third quarter produced at a pace that supports a normal fourth quarter; the prior 49.51 Mt full-year target would need a further inventory draw and a rail step-up. The build is set out in section three. Second, the realised ratio is 0.46, measured on coal revenue only, correcting a modest double count of the non-coal book. Third, the capped power-station share is 0.35, derived from the PLN group's disclosed revenue share and the fact that PLN pays below the average, so its volume share must be higher. Fourth, the bull adds no tonnage, because the base already runs at the approved target [S3, S11].

Two cautions are now quantified rather than asserted. The implied fourth quarter carries IDR3,156.9bn of net profit, a 17.6% net margin and a coal ASP 12.0% above the nine-month average, because the deck's dated full-year benchmark embeds its fourth-quarter forward; holding the fourth quarter at the nine-month price gives FY2026E net profit of IDR6,295.9bn, DPS of Rp328 and a dividend-capacity anchor of Rp2,781 [S0, S11]. And the Banko Barat permit expires on 9 April 2027: it produced 7.62 Mt in the last full year, 16.5% of Tanjung Enim's output, and 83.9% of the DCF's present value sits after that term ends. A permanent loss of that block would cut the life DCF by 11.2%; no renewal application is disclosed [S7, S19, S20].

Three operating items remain noted, not valued: the 2027 production plan has been filed with domestic supply first [S19, S20], PTBA has applied to the energy ministry for approval to keep using its own mining contractor under the new affiliate-services rule [S19], and it is preparing the Ombilin reactivation beside the UNESCO-listed Sawahlunto heritage area [S22]. The Ombilin table carries 102 Mt of resources and 0 Mt of reserves (F96, F97), so it is a resource option outside the 2,883 Mt reserve base and is not valued; no reactivation capex, tonnage or schedule is published [S7, S22].

The export channel, the subject of the last update, stands. From 1 January 2027 coal, palm oil and ferro-alloy exports may be handled only by the state exporter PT DSI, under PP 24/2026 and its implementing trade regulation; registered-exporter permits run only to the end of 2026, and through the transition exporters keep their permits but must file contracts, shipment documents and data with DSI [S12]. The regulation's transition article sets out that reporting duty [S14]. The change touches the export half of PTBA's book: exports were 48.5% of nine-month volume, sold to Bangladesh, Vietnam, India, Cambodia and Thailand [S11]. It changes who handles the export documents, not the sales contract — the government says existing contracts continue [S15]. DSI states it does not take a margin and will charge only a service fee, whose size is not published [S16], and PTBA says it is aligning electronic reporting with customs and the DSI platform while asking for clear procedures and contract terms [S13]. We therefore load no fee and cut no volume; inventing either would be an unsourced change. The risk we do carry is timing: the industry association warns that if the permit handover is treated as paperwork, coal may not be exportable on the first day [S12]. That is a first-quarter risk to the export half, set out in the risks and monitoring sections, not a base-case number.

What the nine months changed. The print is a large earnings beat and a clear volume miss. Net profit reached IDR4,410.0bn, revenue IDR35,200.0bn and EBITDA IDR7,190.0bn, with the average selling price up 18.0% and cost of revenue almost flat at IDR27,940.0bn, while sales fell to 32.23 Mt and production to 34.41 Mt [S11]. The profit surge is price-led and cost-disciplined, not the volume recovery the company's plan assumed, and we treat it that way.

Three inputs now carry the model, each sourced to the print. First, the delivery path: nine-month sales of 32.23 Mt against production of 34.41 Mt left a 2.18 Mt inventory build, and the third quarter produced at a pace that supports a normal fourth quarter; this year therefore takes 47.00 Mt, which is the nine months plus a fourth quarter at the third-quarter production pace, with the build carried as inventory rather than assumed sold [S11]. From next year we hold 49.50 Mt and 49.50 Mt — the company's 2026 target, filed for 2027 but not yet approved — and the report states plainly that this is the 2026 target held forward, not an approved 2027 plan; a delivered run-rate of 46.00 Mt would cut the target by 3.7% [S19, S20]. The bull adds no tonnage: the base is already at the approved target [S3, S11]. Second, the realised ratio: coal revenue — disclosed revenue less the small non-coal book — over 32.23 Mt of sales, against the coal deck's nine-month Newcastle average translated at the deck's rupiah, gives 0.46; the ratio interpolates to 0.50 next year and returns to the last-actual calibration of 0.52 from the third forecast year [S0, S5, S11]. Third, the cost split: we take the measured strip ratio of 5.63 — the nine-month actual of 5.59 against the company's target — and re-derive the non-mining cost per tonne so the full-year total still ties to the nine-month run-rate, with the fuel inflation of 36.0% carried by the model's fuel link [S11]. No value comes from the horizon: the engine's life-end test stops the DCF well before it, so the horizon setting changes nothing we claim [S5, S7].

We still withhold the reverse-DCF variant view. The engine's whole-path override does not reproduce the coal deck's long-run escalation — an identity multiplier flattens the years after the explicit forecast — so any multiplier solved against it sits off the base path; that is an engine issue, escalated to the owner, and we will restore the reverse DCF when the engine reproduces the base. Instead we compare the target with our own scenarios: it sits above the base-scenario value of Rp4,434 and below the bull of Rp8,959, and the bull contributes a little under half of the probability-weighted target [S0, S5].

The honest caution is better documented now. The realised ratio compressed as the benchmark rallied, the volume plan is running short, and the dividend-capacity anchor of Rp3,305 a share sits -33.0% against the DCF because it capitalises near-term earnings and the payout, not the reserve [S5, S6, S11]. We carry that gap in the scenarios.

Bukit Asam is one of the oldest coal enterprises in the archipelago, its Tanjung Enim pits worked
since the colonial era and nationalised after independence. Indonesian thermal coal is a seaborne
swing-supply industry: the country is among the world's largest exporters, its product is mostly
medium-calorific, and its domestic power fleet consumes a mandated share of national output at
administered prices. Calorific content, transport distance and the government reference price, not
company branding, set what a tonne earns.

PTBA is an integrated Indonesian coal company, mining open-pit thermal coal around Tanjung Enim in South Sumatra with smaller operations elsewhere, and running coal transport and port infrastructure alongside the mines [S7]. Its product slate runs from a low-calorific product to a high-calorific one, with the bulk of the blend in the medium grade, represented in our model by a calorific value of 4,600 kcal/kg [S7]. It also carries downstream, power and green-business arms and holds its producing permits as IUP Operasi Produksi, with the Tanjung Enim Air Laya block under a permit dated 2020 [S7].

Sales are split between the domestic market and exports — 16.62 Mt domestic against 15.61 Mt exported in the nine months, a domestic share of 51.5% — with the export book going to Bangladesh, Vietnam, India, Cambodia and Thailand [S11, S20]; from January 2027 that book must clear through the state exporter PT DSI [S12]. The company's advantage is integration: mine-mouth rail and two dedicated coal ports give it a lower delivered cost than a mine without its own corridor, the moat that lets a medium-calorific producer earn a margin [S7]. Its weakness is product quality and a thin per-tonne margin at trough prices.

Volume grew in the last full year, with production and purchases of 47.19 Mt and sales of 45.43 Mt, but the current year has reversed: nine-month production was 34.41 Mt and sales 32.23 Mt, both below the prior year, with transport volume down further at 27.08 Mt [S7, S11]. Management attributes the earnings growth to production recovery in the third quarter, a stronger sales mix and cost discipline, and still guides to a production target of 49.55 Mt for the year, with third-quarter production up 17.0% on the previous quarter and sales up 2.0% [S11, S17, S20]. A share buyback has been under review since October 2026, with no regulatory disclosure yet; we treat it as a catalyst, not as value [S2].

Three operating items sit outside the numbers this round. The company has filed its 2027 production plan with the energy ministry, saying it will put domestic supply first while it watches export opportunities, and that timely approval is what lets it plan logistics, contractor needs and commercial terms [S19, S20]. It has asked the ministry to approve the continued use of PT Satria Bahana Sarana, its own mining contractor, under the new affiliate-services rule; the contractor is consolidated, so the approval is a compliance gate rather than a margin channel [S19, S7]. And it is preparing the reactivation of its Ombilin mine in West Sumatra, where it says the environmental assessment and operating boundaries are being drawn around the UNESCO-listed Sawahlunto coal-mining heritage area and nearby settlements; no tonnage, capex or schedule has been published, and the annual report's resource table carries 102 Mt of resources beside 0 Mt of reserves for Ombilin, so we hold it as a resource option outside the 2,883 Mt reserve base we value rather than as value [S7, S22].

Indonesia's thermal-coal industry is a large, export-led swing supplier with a policy-managed domestic market. National production fell to 790 Mt in the last full year, and the government manages supply through the annual work-and-budget plan: most of the 2026 quota was approved at an aggregate level near the prior-year run-rate after an earlier proposal to tighten it sharply [S7, S9, S10]. PTBA's own plan was approved without a volume cut, but the nine months show that permits and execution are separate constraints [S3, S11]. The 2027 cycle is now open: PTBA has filed its plan and says the national target is the ministry's call, so the approval calendar, not only the quota, is a policy gate for next year's volume [S19, S20].

The domestic-market obligation requires producers to sell a fixed share of output domestically, with a standing US$70/t nominal ceiling on power-station coal in the reviewed coal deck [S0]. It binds in the base case as the deck's benchmark rises through it late in the forecast, on the power-station part of the domestic book we model; charging the cap to the whole domestic book would be the harsher reading, and the size of the capped share is set out in section four. The royalty regime is the other structural lever: as an IUP holder PTBA pays the progressive production royalty, banded on the government's coal reference price and higher on higher-calorific tonnage, but its actual book mixes grades and domestic and export tonnes, so the effective rate it pays is the blended one we model [S5, S6].

The export channel is a further structural lever. Under PP 24/2026 and Permendag 15/2026, strategic-resource exports — coal, palm oil and ferro-alloy — may be handled only by the state exporter PT DSI from 1 January 2027; registered-exporter permits lapse at the end of 2026, and during the transition exporters keep their own permits but must report export documents, sales contracts and shipment data to DSI through an integrated system [S12, S14]. The government says existing export contracts continue, and DSI states it takes no margin and will charge a service fee for services such as export inspection, although the enabling regulation lets it set a margin it judges reasonable [S15, S16]. For PTBA, whose exports were 48.5% of nine-month volume [S11], this moves the export paperwork rather than the commercial contract — unless the fee becomes a levy or the handover slips. The industry association's concern is the second: if the permit transition is treated as administration, coal may not be exportable on the first day [S12].

Competitive position. PTBA is a mid-tier national producer by volume and a top-tier holder of reserves, with a reserve base the annual report puts in the billions of tonnes across its permits [S7]. Its integration along rail and port is the moat, but the same integration makes it capital-heavy and exposes it to rail and port availability — transport volume falling faster than sales in the nine months is a reminder that the corridor itself can be the constraint [S11]. Five forces: supplier power moderate, buyer power high because the domestic fleet is mandated and price-capped, substitutes rising slowly, entry barred by permits, rivalry intense in the seaborne market [S7].

Cost position. The moat is a cost position, and the annual report gives the only public curve anchor: citing Wood Mackenzie's Thermal Coal Review 2026, it places today's Newcastle price near the global marginal production cost, around the 75th percentile of the cost curve [S7]. PTBA's own LK-calibrated coal cash cost is 39.3 dollars a tonne — the nine-month run-rate carried in the model at the deck's rupiah [S5] — a fraction of that marginal cost, so on the disclosed curve the company sits in the lowest quartile. That is the trough-survival argument: a first-quartile cash cost is what lets a producer keep paying through the cycle, and it is why the bear case here is a price and volume case, not a solvency case. The reserve base is 2,883 Mt, a reserve life of 58.2 years at the 49.50 Mt plan [S7].

The commodity frame. The house coal deck prices Newcastle f.o.b. through a mean-reverting path, with a war-premium year folding back toward a through-cycle marker of US$105/t — the deck's long-run anchor for 6,000 kcal NAR thermal coal, set against the World Bank Pink Sheet's history [S0] — well below today's spot of US$150/t, and the government reference price following it down [S0]. That forward path already carries the price softness the trigger article flags for next year; we do not add a second, unsourced cut on top of it [S0]. The macro desk's rupiah view is mildly weakening, which translates dollar coal revenue into more rupiah against a rupiah cost base [S0]. Both frame the valuation; we do not re-forecast them.

Actual against forecast. The nine months delivered revenue of IDR35,200.0bn, reported EBITDA of IDR7,190.0bn and net profit of IDR4,410.0bn [S11]. Two definitions have to be separated before the print is set against the forecast. The release's EBITDA is the company's own measure and is consistent with including the associate contribution of IDR581.3bn [S11]; our model's EBITDA is an operating measure — operating profit plus depreciation and amortisation — and excludes associates, which we carry below the line. On that reading the nine-month operating EBITDA is IDR7,190.0bn less the IDR581.3bn associate share, and the full-year forecast of IDR11,208.6bn is struck on the operating basis too, so the comparison is like for like [S0, S5, S11]. Net profit bridges the same way: nine-month IDR4,410.0bn less the first half's IDR2,643.4bn leaves the third quarter's contribution, and our full-year forecast of IDR7,566.9bn implies a fourth quarter materially above that third-quarter pace, not near it [S6, S11].

The fourth-quarter step-up is arithmetic from an annual build, not a second quarterly forecast, and it is anchored on the measured inputs rather than on a margin assumption. The full-year volume 47.00 Mt is the nine months' sales of 32.23 Mt plus the third quarter's production run-rate; production ran 34.41 Mt in the nine months and left a 2.18 Mt inventory build, so the fourth-quarter tonnage is carried, not assumed drawn from stock [S11]. The realised ratio 0.46 is the coal-only ratio the nine-month print measures — disclosed revenue less the non-coal book over sales, against the deck's nine-month benchmark translated at the deck's rupiah — and it is applied to the deck's full-year benchmark of 137.00 [S0, S11]. That full-year benchmark embeds the deck's fourth-quarter forward price, which sits above the nine-month average, so the implied fourth-quarter selling price is the deck forward at the same measured ratio; it is the forward that lifts the quarter, not a wider margin [S0]. Filling the nine months from the print therefore loads that price uplift into the residual quarter, and because the cost base is held flat in nominal terms through the explicit years most of it falls through to profit. The result is an implied fourth-quarter net profit of IDR3,156.9bn, a net margin of 17.6% and a coal ASP 12.0% above the nine-month average [S0, S11]. Holding the fourth quarter at the nine-month price instead gives FY2026E net profit of IDR6,295.9bn, DPS of Rp328 and a dividend-capacity anchor of Rp2,781 — about a sixth below the base — and that is the sensitivity a reader should carry if the deck's forward is not realised [S0, S8, S11]. The identical statement is in the assumptions file, so the build and the report cannot drift.

The mix of the beat matters more than its size. Revenue rose on sales that fell to 32.23 Mt because the average selling price rose 18.0%, against a high-calorific benchmark that rose more; cost of revenue rose only marginally to IDR27,940.0bn as the strip ratio fell to 5.59 and the company held operating costs; and the profit line also benefited from lower finance costs of IDR136.5bn and associate income of IDR581.3bn [S11]. The lift from associates and the lower finance cost are below-the-line items the DCF does not capitalise.

The model's finance charge is above the nine-month run-rate, and that is a basis difference rather than a forecast of dearer debt. The engine applies the three-year historical cost of debt to gross debt, which now includes the low-coupon back-to-back facility secured by the export-proceeds placements, while the income earned on those placements sits outside the modelled cash balance [S6, S11]. We take no value from the gap in either direction; it is a small caution inside the target, and the nine-month net finance position is the better read of the year [S11].

Cash conversion is where this update adds evidence. First-half operating cash flow was IDR4,625.7bn [S6] against IDR4,440.0bn for the nine months [S11], so the third quarter absorbed operating cash while profit rose from IDR2,643.4bn in the first half to IDR4,410.0bn for the nine months [S6, S11]. The interim accounts now decompose the swing: total net trade receivables reached IDR5,820.0bn at 30 September, up 47.9% from the year-end level on revenue up 12.4%, and the PLN group alone is IDR2,680.0bn of it, up 119.0% [S21]. That is the divergence flag in our earnings-quality screen — receivables growing several times faster than revenue — confirmed, and we classify it as optics-class rather than manipulation-class: the balance is disclosed, concentrated in a state power counterparty, and only IDR269.5bn of the book has aged beyond the longest past-due bucket [S21]. Against nine-month net profit of IDR4,410.0bn, operating cash of IDR4,440.0bn means the year-to-date conversion is broadly complete; the third quarter is timing, not a trend. The base's negative working-capital ratio is not an imposed release: the data pack's 30 September balance sheet itself carries negative net working capital, so the three-year-average ratio the model holds is the observed level, and the working-capital release is the arithmetic of applying it to a larger revenue base. The stress below is the opposite case, turning the gross receivables build into a positive net working-capital ratio; it is disclosed, not carried, because the latest balance sheet and the three-year average do not support it as the modal path [S0, S21]. What we cannot yet say is whether the PLN balance unwinds by December: that is the test at the full-year accounts, and if it does not, both the forecast working-capital assumption and the dividend-capacity anchor need re-underwriting [S6, S11, S21]. The dividend-capacity anchor is where that matters: holding the receivables build structurally, with net working capital at the nine-month run-rate rather than unwinding, cuts FY2026E free cash flow to IDR2,558.2bn from IDR4,543.7bn and lowers the life DCF by 2.2% [S21]. The modelled DPS and the anchor do not move, because they follow the payout rule, so the strain would show in cash cover rather than in the anchor a reader sees. The realised-price and royalty data still do not point to a revenue-recognition issue [S11].

The last full year was a thin-margin year, and the restatement still drives it: revenue of IDR42,651.7bn, EBITDA of IDR5,222.2bn after the audited depreciation and amortisation charge of IDR2,014.1bn replaces the data pack's fragment, and royalties of IDR4,322.7bn, about a tenth of coal revenue [S5]. The effective royalty rate is the one we carry into the forecast, consistent with the interim accounts and with the nine-month release's nearly flat cost of revenue [S5, S6, S11].

The balance sheet remains strong but its shape changed. At the end of September cash was IDR4,890.0bn and bank loans IDR4,210.0bn, the latter including a back-to-back facility secured by export-proceeds placements [S11]. Those placements sit in the investing outflow of IDR3,500.0bn, outside cash and equivalents [S11]; netting them against the loans leaves net liquid assets above the data pack's cash line, so the operating move carries no separate bridge item. The engine values the company off the data pack's 30 September 2026 balance sheet, and the bridge carries no post-balance-sheet item: the FY2025 dividend of IDR1,310.0bn was declared 11 June and paid 10 July 2026, before that date, so its payment is already in the 30 September cash and deducting the payable again would double count [S6, S11]. The equity-accounted stakes are carried at the same book value [S6].

Forecasts. We reconcile the nine months with a fourth quarter at the third-quarter production pace, hold the approved 2026 target from next year — as a target, not an approved 2027 plan — and hold unit costs flat in nominal terms through FY2030E and escalate them with Indonesian inflation after that, with dollar prices escalating on US inflation — the nominal-consistent treatment the house method requires [S0]. We say flat in nominal, not in real terms: at Indonesian inflation the explicit years carry a gentle real decline, which is the more optimistic reading and is the one the model actually holds. The realised ratio keeps the 2026 compression in the first year and returns to the last-actual calibration thereafter, so the long-run value is not set by a forecast-year spike or trough [S5, S11]. Capital spending is set to the company's IDR3,640.0bn budget for the year — the per-tonne rate plus a budget top-up — rather than the lower volume-times-rate figure, so committed project spend is not cut by the volume miss; the difference is a fraction of the per-share DCF of Rp4,929 [S11].

The forecast peaks with the deck's near-term price years and reverts with the benchmark, but the terminal years are not a reserve-life perpetuity: the DMO ceiling clips the capped power-station tonnes late in the forecast — it is the reviewed coal deck's policy assumption, held flat in nominal terms with no escalation [S0] — so free cash flow fades before the reserve is exhausted and the life-end test stops the DCF at FY2054E rather than at the reserve year. There is no terminal growth rate: the DCF runs on reserves and stops when marginal value turns negative. The excluded tail is a modelling convention, not a forecast, which is why the bull lifts the ceiling with the benchmark so the capped tonnes stay economic; that cap lift is a real difference between the base and the bull, and the base does not pay for an administrative price rise the state has not made [S0].

Why this method set. PTBA is a life-of-asset commodity producer, so the primary method is a life-of-reserve DCF at the coal deck's through-cycle prices, not a spot multiple. Valuing a cyclical on current-year earnings is the classic procyclical error; the NAV uses the deck's mean-reverting path, and the other anchors are secondary — real weight, but a minority of it. The house weighting is 60% to the life DCF, 25% to EV/EBITDA and 15% to dividend capacity [S5, S6].
Cost of capital.

The build uses the risk-free rate from the house macro deck, the mature-market equity premium and Indonesia's country risk premium, an unlevered beta from the industry regression median (0.80) re-levered for the group's small net debt, and a dollar cost of debt; the resulting weighted average cost of capital is 11.2%, applied to the reserve-life cash flows [S5, S6].
Primary method.

The DCF discounts free cash flow to the firm over the reserve life, adds the 30 September 2026 net cash the engine reads from the data pack, brings in the equity-accounted investments at book, and deducts minorities; the bridge carries no dividend-payable item because the FY2025 dividend was paid on 10 July 2026, before that balance-sheet date [S0, S6]. The table's bridge lines show the exact figures. That book is not a black box: most of it is HBAP, the South Sumatra mine-mouth power venture selling to PLN under a long-term purchase agreement, carried at IDR7,700.4bn against venture net assets of IDR17,111.9bn; BPI, the Lahat mine-mouth plant, at IDR2,927.2bn against IDR4,899.1bn; and a small rail venture at IDR5.4bn [S6]. The carrying values are the group's equity-method share of net assets, and the interim accounts disclose no impairment or pending review, so we treat book as the LK's own measure of recoverable value rather than an independent mark; on the nine-month associate run-rate of IDR581.3bn the total implies a low-to-mid-teens earnings multiple, which is what a depreciation-heavy, PPA-backed power asset looks like on earnings, not evidence the stake is overstated [S6]. The HBAP shares are pledged to the export-import bank that funded the project — a structure point we note rather than price [S6]. One definitional note: the modelled FY2025A net-debt history excludes the current maturities of long-term bank borrowings, which is why it sits a little below a leaf-by-leaf rebuild of the December balance sheet; the valuation reads the data pack's 30 September 2026 balance sheet, and the equity-accounted stakes are carried at the last detailed disclosure's book, so the exclusion carries no value effect [S0, S6]. It carries no terminal value because the reserves are finite. The engine's life-end test stops the DCF at the point of maximum cumulative value. In the base case the stop is set by the fixed nominal DMO ceiling clipping the capped tonnes late in the forecast, so the DCF does not run to the full reserve year, and the long tail of a very large reserve base is not counted when it would subtract value [S0, S7]. The life the DCF runs rests on the permits as much as on the reserve: the nearest producing permit, Banko Barat, runs only to 9 April 2027 — just inside the next financial year — with Muara Tiga Besar to 29 August 2029 and Air Laya to 31 December 2030, so FY2027E volume itself depends on a renewal falling inside the forecast year; the annual report says the company renews its IUPs on time but discloses no application, and neither the nine-month release nor the 2027-plan reporting mentions one [S7, S19, S20]. 83.9% of the DCF's present value sits in the years after FY2027E, and the block itself produced 7.62 Mt in the last full year, 16.5% of Tanjung Enim's output; permanent non-renewal would lower the life DCF by 11.2% and the target by less than that [S7]. Renewal is the largest single assumption in the valuation, not a footnote — a reader who does not accept timely renewal should not accept most of the target [S0, S7].
Cross-checks.

The EV/EBITDA anchor applies a blend of the peer median and PTBA's own five-year average, 5.12x, to the last actual year's EBITDA of IDR5,222.2bn, giving an anchor -29.7% against the primary DCF [S5, S6]. We name the metric plainly because FY2025A is a trough: the same multiple on the forecast year's IDR11,208.6bn would land above the DCF, so the gap is cycle position, not an asset-value signal, and we do not read it as the reserve being overvalued. The dividend-capacity anchor capitalises the modelled distribution at the sector's yield — the anchor the market most often uses for Indonesian coal names — and it lands -33.0% against the DCF. The dividend anchor is the lower of the two and the gap widened with the nine-month update, and we explain it rather than assert a band: it capitalises a distribution of Rp394 a share struck on earnings that carry the compressed 2026 realised ratio, while the life-of-reserve DCF runs the deck's full price path over the whole reserve life. These two are not footnotes: they carry 25.0% and 15.0% of the target, and both divergences are about where in the price cycle each method looks, not about the asset; the house weights favour the DCF [S5, S7].

Sensitivity. We withhold the benchmark-and-rupiah grid this round. Every grid that shocks the benchmark runs through the engine's whole-path override, which flattens the deck's post-explicit escalation, so the centre cell does not reconcile with the target and we will not publish a table we cannot stand behind [S0]. The engine's volume-and-cost-intensity grid does not touch the benchmark, is clean, and its centre reproduces the base value, so the ranking below rests on a run we can defend [S0]. The rank order is unchanged: a life-of-reserve value is most sensitive to the realised price and the rupiah, and least to volume at the margin — an inventory-of-reserves business, not a growth business [S0, S5]. The one judgement the price grids do not settle is how much of the domestic book sits under the cap. We charge it to the power-station share, hold that share in both tails, and let the scenarios move the cap level instead. The share is now derived rather than assumed: the PLN group accounted for IDR14,429.2bn of last-actual revenue, and IDR10,803.0bn, or 30.7% of consolidated revenue, in the nine months [S5, S21]. Because PLN pays below the average, its volume share must exceed its revenue share, and we take 0.35 at the low end of the disclosed range rather than the half-domestic heuristic of the prior round. The value effect is small but real: raising the share by ten points lowers the life DCF by 1.1%, while removing the cap entirely would add 6.8% to the life DCF — the reserve-tail unlock we show here but do not pay in the base or the bull [S0, S7]. A higher share than ours would lower the capped tonnage's realisation and the value, and the sensitivity is bounded on both sides by the tails' cap cut and lift rather than by a second grid.

Royalty tail. The base charges the LK's effective rate flat through the whole path, which is the most-likely rate for a domestic-heavy, mixed-calorific book that pays a blended rate today. The schedule is progressive, though, and the deck's tail benchmark is far above today's, so the flat rate could understate the royalty in the late years. Running the deck's mid-band IUP schedule on the HBA reference instead of the flat rate — the conservative tail test — lowers the life DCF by roughly a tenth from Rp4,929 [S0]. We do not carry it in the base because no observed year charges that band, and the interim accounts show the same blended rate; the sensitivity is disclosed so a reader who expects the tail to be taxed at the schedule can see the cost. The bull is not credited with the banded schedule, so the flat rate flatters the bull rather than the base if the tail is wrong [S5, S6].

Spot versus through-cycle. The same reserve life valued with the benchmark held at today's spot print, in real terms, is Rp15,151 a share, against the through-cycle Rp4,929 — well above the base case, and a reminder of how much of the number is cycle position [S0, S7]. That gap is not a second valuation: it says the tape is discounting the base path hard, but it also says a model that capitalised spot would be pricing the war premium in perpetuity, which is the procyclical error the method card warns against. We carry the through-cycle number as the primary and disclose the spot case as the upper bound.

What the price implies. We do not publish a reverse-DCF multiplier this round, for the same engine reason: a multiplier solved on the flattened path is not on the base path [S0]. The directional reading does not depend on the grid, and it is stated plainly: at Rp3,030 the market prices the equity at about three-fifths of the life-of-reserve DCF of Rp4,929, so it is discounting well over a third of the base path before any probability weighting [S0, S5]. We will restore the reverse DCF — the implied benchmark price that today's price supports — as soon as the engine reproduces the deck's long-run path; until then this ratio is the substitute. The target is above the base-scenario value of Rp4,434 and below the bull of Rp8,959, and the market price of Rp3,030 sits between the bear-scenario value of Rp1,748 and the base, closer to the bear: the market is assigning more weight to the downside state than the quarter we carry, and the gap to our base is a probability disagreement rather than a different view of the reserve value [S5, S6]. Calibration note: re-pricing the last actual year at its own benchmark, volume, realised ratio and rupiah reproduces the LK's EBITDA to within a couple of per cent, with the residual carried by the cost split, which is struck on the nine-month run-rate and the current fuel basis; the engine's headline gap is wider because it prices FY2025A's volume and benchmark at the FY2026E realised ratio and rupiah [S5, S11].
Downside risks, with our view of likelihood and impact.

items: **Commodity price (high likelihood, high impact).** The benchmark reverting through the deck's
long-run marker below spot is the base case, and a deeper oversupply — Chinese and Indian restarts,
relaxed Indonesian supply discipline — takes realised prices below our path. The per-tonne margin is
thin at trough prices, so small price moves are large earnings moves [S0].
**Realisation compression (high likelihood, medium impact).** The nine-month record shows the
medium-calorific book captured much less of the benchmark rally than the high-calorific index, so
the compression we now carry could persist beyond the next year rather than unwind [S11].
**Volume execution (high likelihood, high impact).** Nine-month sales ran well below the plan and
transport volumes fell faster, so the recovery we assume is a forecast, not a delivered fact; a
repeat of the first nine months removes the second-half volume the plan needs [S11].
**Domestic policy and quota (medium likelihood, high impact).** A tightened RKAB ceiling, a delayed
approval of the 2027 plan, or a domestic-market obligation applied at a lower price, would cut
volume or realisation. PTBA's own RKAB was approved without a cut, but national policy has swung
before, and the 2027 plan is filed rather than approved [S9, S10, S19, S20].
**Export-channel transition (medium likelihood, medium impact).** From January 2027 every export
tonne must clear through PT DSI; exports were 48.5% of nine-month volume, so a go-live
slip stops the export half, and a service fee takes a slice of realised price. As arithmetic: each
point of fee is charged on 48.5% of the forecast revenue of
IDR53,179.9bn, with the after-tax profit and DCF effect following in proportion —
small per point, but a levy on nearly half the book. We carry no fee in any case because no rate is
published: the bear is deliberately fee-free and this sensitivity is the substitute [S16]. The
industry association warns the permit handover could halt shipments on day one, and the enabling
regulation lets DSI set a margin it judges reasonable [S12, S16]; the bear's volume cut carries
that stoppage, as set out below. PTBA says it is aligning its systems and asks for clear
procedures [S13].
**Currency (medium likelihood, medium impact).** A sharply stronger rupiah compresses the dollar
revenue translated into rupiah while the cost base stays in rupiah; the reverse is the tailwind in
our forecast [S0].
**Cost inflation (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Fuel prices rose 36.0% in the nine
months and offset the lower strip ratio; a sustained fuel price or a higher strip ratio as pits
deepen would raise cash cost per tonne [S11].
**Working capital (medium likelihood, medium impact).** The third quarter absorbed operating cash
while profit rose, and the interim accounts show why: net trade receivables have grown several
times faster than revenue, led by the PLN group, although the past-due tail is small [S21]. Held
structurally, the build would cut FY2026E free cash flow to IDR2,558.2bn and the life DCF by
2.2%, with the strain appearing in cash cover rather than in the payout-rule anchor
[S21]. A year-end that does not unwind the balance would turn the earnings beat into a receivables
story and test the dividend the capacity anchor capitalises [S6, S11, S21].
**Governance and related parties (low likelihood, medium impact).** A state-controlled issuer with a
majority related-party revenue book carries the modal Indonesian value-destruction risk; the flows
are disclosed and priced off third-party terms, but they are large [S5, S7]. The new
affiliate-contractor approval is the item to watch: it keeps a consolidated contractor inside the
group, so the test is whether its rate stays at arm's length [S19].
**Project and heritage execution (low likelihood, low-to-medium impact).** The Ombilin reactivation
sits beside a UNESCO-listed heritage area and still needs its environmental assessment and
operating boundaries; a delay costs an option, not base-case value [S22].

blocks.text: Scenarios.

Bear: the state takes a larger share of a state-owned producer — a work-and-budget cut toward the lower national ceiling the government proposed before approving the higher one, or a tighter domestic-market obligation at the capped power price — while the benchmark rolls back through the deck's long-run marker and the medium-calorific book keeps the realised price a fifth weaker on the company's own ratio, so the whole price path, escalation included, moves down with it. Volume is cut about five million tonnes below the base, the price cap is cut a fifth below the deck's level — the mirror of the bull's lift — so the fixed nominal ceiling clips the capped tonnes harder and the payout falls to the FY2025 trough ratio as earnings fall. That volume cut carries the January handover too: a quarter's export tonnage lost at go-live sits inside the five million tonnes, so the policy event is in the number rather than beside it [S12]. The volume risk is visible in the actuals: the nine months ran below the plan, so the bear is a continuation of what has been delivered, not a hypothesis [S9, S10, S11]. Bull: a sustained war-premium holds the benchmark above the long-run marker and the realised price is shocked a fifth above the base path — the mirror of the bear's cut, and a scenario boundary rather than a claim that the ratio returns to an observed level, because the three published years do not bound a tail — as the medium-calorific spread narrows and the export share rises [S5, S11]. The price cap is lifted a fifth with the benchmark here — the mirror of the bear's cut — so the capped tonnes stay economic a little longer, and the payout returns to the boom-year ratio PTBA's own record demonstrates. Volume adds no tonnage: the base already runs at the approved 2026 target from next year, and no approved headroom above it is disclosed, so the upside is carried on realised price, the mirror cap lift and payout, not on above-target tonnes [S3, S11]. The two tails shock the same four drivers — realised price, the DMO cap, payout and volume — with mirrored moves on the price and the cap; the volume shock is asymmetric because the bear continues the delivered nine-month shortfall while the bull is bounded by the approved target, and that asymmetry is the one sourced exception [S9, S10, S11]. The full reserve-tail unlock from removing the cap is not paid here: run on its own it adds 6.8% to the life DCF and was the source of the one-tailed target the prior round carried, so it sits in the sensitivity discussion instead [S0]. The tails move the cap level a fifth either way rather than the capped share, so the mirror is exact on the policy price.

The target is above our own base scenario but now below the primary DCF. At the house probabilities the bull contributes the largest single share of the weighted target on its quarter weight — realised price and payout do most of that work, with the mirrored cap lift a minor increment — with the base a similar share and the bear the remainder; the bull carries Rp8,959 against the base of Rp4,434, so the rating leans on a state in which the realised ratio and the payout recover and the price holds [S5, S8]. We consider that state as likely as the bear, which is why the target sits above the base; after the scenario mirror it sits just below the primary DCF of Rp4,929 rather than above it, so no part of the target any longer rests on an administrative-price rise the state has not made [S0]. It is a probability-weighted number, not a base-case number, and it sits below the bull.

The optionality the base case does not pay for. The bull now carries the higher payout, which is how we quantify the distribution optionality rather than asserting it: a payout back at the boom-year ratio flows straight into the dividend-capacity anchor and is worth the bull's Rp8,959 against the base [S7, S8]. The buyback itself stays outside both tails: it is under board review with no regulatory disclosure, so its size, timing and price are unknown and a share-count cut would be invented; the decision that would make it value is a filed buyback struck below the DCF of Rp4,929 [S2]. Beyond the reserve base we value, the annual report carries 5,713 Mt of resources against the 2,883 Mt reserve base, including a large un-developed block at Banko Tengah; the Ombilin row carries 102 Mt of resources and 0 Mt of reserves, so it is a resource option outside the base, with undisclosed reactivation capex [S7, S22]. Converting even part of the inventory would extend the modelled life rather than change near-term cash flows, so we treat it as upside prose, not value [S7].

Signposts that would change our view: the realised ratio recovering while the benchmark rolls over; a formal buyback or higher dividend policy; an RKAB cut applied to PTBA itself; a rupiah break either way; delivered volume close to the full-year plan; any sign of a lower domestic price; and a DSI service fee that becomes a material levy on export revenue, or an export stoppage at go-live [S2, S8, S10, S11, S12, S16].

Ownership and control. PTBA is state-controlled: the government holds the special Dwiwarna share and the MIND ID mining holding owns 65.9% of the register, with the public holding the balance and a small treasury position [S7]. Strategy follows the holding's direction, and major corporate actions need board and shareholder approval — the structure that governs the buyback now under review [S2, S7].

Related parties. Related-party revenue is large because state entities are related parties under the Indonesian accounting standards; the audited note puts coal revenue from related parties at a majority of coal sales in the last actual year [S5]. This is a disclosure-quality point rather than a red flag — the flows are to the domestic power fleet and other state buyers — but we do not take arm's length on trust, because the same state sets both the domestic price ceiling and the reference price that bands the royalty. The test we apply is whether the blended realised price the company actually achieves sits below the government reference price for its calorific band: the nine-month record shows the realised price below the contemporaneous benchmark and the royalty charged at the blended schedule rate, which is what arm's-length state pricing under the domestic-market rules looks like [S5, S6, S11]. A new related-party item belongs here: PTBA has asked the energy ministry to approve continued use of PT Satria Bahana Sarana, its own mining contractor subsidiary, under the ministry's new affiliate-services rule [S19, S7]. Because the contractor is consolidated, its margin already sits inside group cost rather than being extracted from it, so the approval is a compliance gate; the question we keep is whether the contracted rate is at arm's length against third-party mining contractors, which the consolidated accounts blur [S19]. The company states it has no material conflict-of-interest transactions [S7]. The reclamation and mine-closure obligation is a balance-sheet provision and is reflected in the accounts; it is not an incremental DCF charge because the life-end test truncates the model ahead of reserve exhaustion [S5, S6].

Audit and reporting. The last full year's consolidated statements carry an unmodified opinion from KAP Purwantono, Susanti dan Surja, a member firm of Ernst & Young Global, with no special GMS status, going-concern notation or qualification [S5]. The nine-month figures are unaudited and reach us through press summaries of the interim accounts, so we weight the audited annual figures and expect the usual fourth-quarter true-ups [S11, S21].

Dividends. The stated policy is to distribute at least a set share of net profit under the IPO prospectus unless the GMS decides otherwise, with a long record of paying above that floor [S7]. The FY2025 book dividend was approved at the June-2026 annual GMS at IDR1,310.0bn, a payout well above the policy floor but below the boom-year payouts [S7, S8]. Our modelled payout sits between the floor and that record, and the stronger 2026 earnings lift the modelled distribution to Rp394 a share [S8, S11].

ESG exposures. PTBA's material issues are land and biodiversity around the Tanjung Enim and Kalimantan pits, mine-closure and reclamation liabilities, water and tailings management, and the transition risk of a thermal-coal franchise. It carries a reclamation and mine-closure provision and reports sustainability and climate disclosures alongside the annual report, and it is a large regional employer running community programmes [S5, S7]. The Ombilin reactivation adds a heritage dimension: the mine sits beside the UNESCO-listed Sawahlunto coal-mining heritage area, and the company says its environmental assessment and operating boundaries are being drawn to protect the historic town, public facilities and nearby settlements [S22]. The transition is the structural risk: a net-zero path and the grid's renewables build eventually shrink the domestic thermal market, and the reserve life we value reaches well into that horizon.

Dated catalysts are in the frontmatter: fourth-quarter delivery against target, a buyback decision, the January go-live of the PT DSI export channel, the annual GMS that sets the FY2026 dividend, and the 2027 work-and-budget plan, which the company has now filed with domestic supply first [S2, S8, S10, S11, S12, S19].

Between updates we monitor a short list. First, the price side: the Newcastle benchmark and the government reference price off the coal deck, spot against the deck's path, and the rupiah off the macro deck [S0]. Second, the company's own delivery: quarterly volumes and realised price against the plan and against the ratio we have calibrated, the stripping ratio and the cash cost per tonne against the last actual, and the transport volumes on the Tanjung Enim corridor [S11]. Third, the cash side: the full-year bridge from operating cash flow to profit, and whether the PLN-group receivable unwinds by the year-end accounts [S6, S11, S21]. Fourth, the policy side: the 2027 plan and RKAB decision, any change to the domestic-market obligation or the price ceiling, any royalty-order change, and whether the Banko Barat renewal is filed or decided before the April term end [S3, S5, S7, S9, S10, S19]. Fifth, the export channel: the first post-transition clearances after January 2027, the DSI service-fee schedule, any margin determination under PP 24/2026, and whether PTBA's export contracts are novated cleanly [S12, S13, S16]. Sixth, the corporate items: the affiliate-contractor approval, any published Ombilin tonnage, capex or schedule, and any filed buyback [S19, S22, S2].

The number that would move our rating most is the realised price-to-benchmark ratio recovering while the benchmark rolls over: that is the bull case, it is not in the base case, and we would re-underwrite on the first report of it [S5, S7]. The second is a formal buyback or a higher dividend policy, which would lift the dividend-capacity anchor that sits below the DCF [S2, S8].

bear.narrative: Newcastle rolls back through the deck's long-run floor as Chinese and Indian mine restarts and relaxed Indonesian RKAB discipline turn the 2025-26 war-premium tightness into oversupply, and the state takes a larger share of a state-owned producer: an RKAB cut toward the ~600 Mt national level the government proposed before approving ~720 Mt, or a tighter DMO at the capped power price, cuts PTBA's volume by about a tenth while its medium-CV, domestic-heavy blend keeps the realised-to-benchmark ratio compressed as the benchmark falls. The realised price is shocked on the company ratio (0.8x) rather than on the benchmark deck, so the whole price path, including its long-run escalation, moves together. The DMO ceiling is cut a fifth below the reviewed deck level — the mirror of the bull's lift — so the fixed nominal cap bites harder and truncates the modelled life earlier, and the dividend steps down to the FY2025 trough payout as earnings fall. The volume cut also carries the transition risk this update exists to examine: a delayed permit handover at the January 2027 DSI go-live would strand a quarter's export tonnage, about the size of the shock, so the policy event is inside the number rather than beside it [S12]. The bear carries no DSI service fee because no rate is published [S16]; the per-point fee sensitivity sits in the report, not in the scenario.

bull.narrative: A sustained war-premium in seaborne thermal coal and Chinese import curbs keep Newcastle above the deck's long-run marker, and the realised price is shocked a fifth above the base path — the mirror of the bear's cut, which takes the realised-to-benchmark ratio above the FY2025A calibration rather than toward it. That is a scenario boundary, not a forecast of an observed ratio: the three published years (FY2023-25) do not bound a tail, and the ratio can rise without any observed level being contradicted if the medium-CV spread narrows and the export share keeps rising. Production holds the approved 49.5 Mt target — the base itself already runs at it from FY2027E — so the bull adds no tonnage and the extra dollars convert into cash against a rupiah cost base that does not move with them. The DMO ceiling is lifted a fifth above the reviewed deck's US$70/t level (S0) — the mirror of the bear's cut — so the capped domestic tonnes stay economic a little longer; the full reserve-tail unlock is shown as a sensitivity in the report, not paid in the base. Royalty stays flat at the LK's effective rate in both tails (no scenario switches to the banded schedule), and the higher distribution PTBA's record demonstrates is paid as the payout returns to its FY2023-24 level. The two tails shock the same four drivers — realised price, volume, the DMO cap and payout — with mirrored moves on the price, cap and payout; the volume shock is asymmetric because the bear continues the delivered shortfall while the bull cannot exceed the approved 49.5 Mt target, and that asymmetry is justified in qc_justifications.
